title: Navaratri (nine nights, nine forms; Durga)
hook: a small red book read aloud before sunrise for nine mornings: three battles, one Goddess, and nine faces

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi in the morning: Krishna, Radha, and a pinch of color. Your line was color closes a distance.

Before sunrise, in a small kitchen in Kolkata, a grandmother sits on a low stool with a red cloth-bound book open on her knees. She reads aloud in Sanskrit, fast and steady, the way you read something you've read every autumn of your life. A lamp burns beside her. She'll do this every morning until the ninth. Inside is the story from day eighty-seven: the gods' light in one blazing form, a lion to ride, a buffalo demon who kept changing shape. Today, the book itself, and the nine faces the nights are kept for.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE, A RED BOOK.` → `READ ALOUD, NINE MORNINGS.` → `THE BOOK AND THE NINE FACES.`

segments.voice: The book is the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a Sanskrit text set inside the Markandeya Purana. Many families read it, or have a priest read it, across the nine nights, sometimes whole, sometimes a part each day. It also goes by Durga Saptashati, the seven hundred, after its traditional count of verses. And it isn't one battle. It's three. In the first, the world is all ocean, Vishnu lies in his cosmic sleep, and two demons, Madhu and Kaitabha, threaten Brahma. Brahma praises the Goddess as that very sleep. She lets go of Vishnu, he wakes, and he fights. The second is the buffalo demon you already know. In the third, two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, send army after army, and a dark, fierce form, Kali, springs from the Goddess's own brow to meet them. Sleep, a warrior on a lion, the dark one from her brow: in the text, all of them are her. Many Hindus honor her in nine forms, the Navadurga, one a night. Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain. Brahmacharini, the young woman in hard discipline. Chandraghanta, with a half-moon like a bell on her forehead. Kushmanda. Skandamata, mother of the war god Skanda. Katyayani, the warrior. Kalaratri, the dark night. Mahagauri, shining and calm. Siddhidatri, who gives perfection. Traditions differ on details and order, but the idea holds: the same power shows up differently on different nights. In the book, she promises the gods she'll come again whenever they call on her in trouble. Nine nights of reading is one way of calling.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA, READ ALOUD.` · `NOT ONE BATTLE, THREE.` · `NINE FORMS, ONE EACH NIGHT.` · `SHE PROMISES TO COME WHEN CALLED.` · then, large: `THE SAME POWER, NINE FACES.`

segments.voice: Ask what today needs from you, the way the Goddess shows a different face each night: the daughter of the mountain, steady and rooted; the student, disciplined, one more page; the warrior who says the hard thing; the mother, gentle with someone small; or just the calm one. Let one face come. Then breathe as that face for a while, and notice how it sits in your shoulders.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept with her book read aloud and a different face honored each night.
Your line: wear it on purpose. Gentle or fierce, every face is hers. That's day one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: During Navaratri many Hindus read or recite the Devi Mahatmya (the Durga Saptashati) across the nine nights and honor the Goddess in nine forms, the Navadurga, one each night, with fasting and prayers; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates victory.

fork.setup: you're Brahma. the world is all ocean, Vishnu is deep in his cosmic sleep, and two demons are coming for you. what do you do?
options: praise the Goddess as Vishnu's sleep, so she lets him wake.
fork.reveal: Brahma praises the Goddess as that very sleep. she lets go of Vishnu, he wakes, and he fights. in the Devi Mahatmya, even sleep is her.

original.note: Sanskrit devīmāhātmya: devī, the Goddess, and māhātmya, greatness, glory.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nine-day holiday about a goddess.
what it means: nine nights of the Goddess, kept with her book read aloud and one of her nine forms honored each night.

what a scholar hears: the Devi Mahatmya, recited as the Durga Saptashati or Chandi Path, is built in three episodes, each led by a different form of the Goddess, and sits inside the Markandeya Purana.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya (Markandeya Purana): ch. 1 (Madhu and Kaitabha; the Goddess as Vishnu's sleep), chs. 2–4 (Mahishasura), chs. 5–10 (Shumbha and Nishumbha; Kali from the brow, ch. 7), the Goddess's promise to return (chs. 4 and 11)
Navadurga (the nine forms honored across Navaratri)

notes: Devi Mahatmya: 'Saptashati, the seven hundred, after its traditional count of verses'; chapters 81–93 of the Markandeya Purana in the common numbering. Confirm.
Recitation of the Devi Mahatmya across Navaratri (whole or in parts, at home or by a priest) varies by region and family. Confirm.

Navadurga order and one-line glosses (Shailaputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri, Siddhidatri) follow the common list (e.g. Devi Kavacham). Confirm.
Kali springs from Ambika's brow in Devi Mahatmya ch. 7 (against Chanda and Munda); the promise to return when called is paraphrased from chs. 4 and 11. Confirm.
The hook's Kolkata grandmother is an illustrative scene, not a claim.
